opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it helps to be really precise about what LEACE actually guarantees, because that shapes how you evaluate it.

LEACE, least-squares concept erasure, gives you a closed-form transformation of the representation with a provable property: after erasure, *no linear classifier* can predict the concept better than a constant predictor that just guesses the base rate. The key theoretical result in the paper is that this condition is equivalent to the class-conditional means of the representation all being equal. Put another way, the cross-covariance between the features and the concept label is zero. Among all transformations that achieve that, LEACE picks the one that changes the representation the least in a mean-squared-error sense. So it's surgical. You remove exactly the linearly available information about the concept and as little else as possible.

The first way to assess it is just to check that guarantee empirically. You train fresh linear probes on the erased representations, and they really do fall to chance. That's not surprising, since it's a theorem, but it's a good sanity check. It also separates LEACE from earlier methods like INLP or RLACE. Those can leave residual linear information, or they damage the representation more than they need to.

The more interesting question is whether the *network itself* stops using the concept. For that we developed what we call concept scrubbing, where you apply LEACE at every layer of a transformer, sequentially, so that later layers can't just reconstruct the concept from earlier residual-stream information. We did this with part-of-speech information in language models like LLaMA and Pythia. Performance degraded noticeably, with perplexity going up quite a bit. To us that's evidence the models genuinely rely on that linearly encoded part-of-speech information, and that erasing it actually takes it away from them rather than being trivially routed around. We also looked at things like gender bias in BERT-style models and found that erasure reduced the model's ability to exploit gender information in downstream tasks.

That said, I want to be honest about the limitations. The guarantee is linear. A nonlinear probe, an MLP for example, can often still recover the concept after LEACE, because information can live in higher-order statistics, in the covariance structure and so on. And a neural network downstream of the erasure point is of course nonlinear, so in principle it could extract that residual information. Scrubbing at every layer mitigates this a lot in practice, but it's not a proof that the network can't use the concept in any form. That's part of why we've done follow-up work on erasing higher-order information, for instance matching class-conditional covariances, which gets you guarantees against quadratic adversaries, though that's harder to do without hurting the representation.

So my overall assessment is this. LEACE is about as good as you can get for *linear* concept erasure. It's provably optimal in that setting, and it's empirically effective at stopping models from relying on linearly represented features. But if your threat model is a powerful nonlinear adversary, or a model that's being fine-tuned to recover the concept, you shouldn't treat linear erasure as a complete solution.

r001.rationale: The response says nonlinear probes can still recover the concept after LEACE because information may remain in higher-order statistics, which downstream nonlinear networks could exploit.

r002.rationale: It reports that language models rely on linearly encoded part-of-speech information, presenting this as evidence from experiments on neural networks.

r003.rationale: The response discusses reducing reliance on linearly represented features, but does not express hope about erasing an optional, nonessential feature.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest way to put it is that LEACE gives you a guarantee, but the guarantee is narrower than people sometimes assume, and I think it's important to be precise about what it is.

What LEACE actually does is find the smallest possible change to your representations, in a least-squares sense, such that no linear classifier can do better than chance at predicting the concept afterwards. And "no linear classifier" is a strong statement. It's not that we fit one probe and it failed. We prove that every linear predictor is reduced to chance accuracy. That's the sense in which it's concept erasure rather than just making the concept harder to find. And it's closed form, it's cheap, you can apply it at every layer during a forward pass, so it's practical.

But the key word is linear. If the network can read the concept off through some nonlinear combination of features, LEACE doesn't rule that out. We were quite careful in the paper not to claim otherwise. And in practice there's a question of how much that matters. Our empirical intuition, and this goes back to the linear representation hypothesis, is that a lot of what transformers actually use downstream is linearly accessible. If you erase it linearly at every layer, you do see the model's behavior change in the way you'd want, for example on the gender bias experiments we ran, or when we erased part-of-speech information and the language model's loss went up in the way you'd predict if it had really been using that information.

So I'd say: strong guarantee against linear reliance, suggestive but not airtight evidence about actual downstream reliance, and genuinely no guarantee about nonlinear recovery. The other caveat I'd add is that erasing a concept everywhere isn't free. There's collateral damage to things that are correlated with the concept, and a model can also just learn to route around the erasure if you train it with LEACE in the loop. We touched on that in the paper, and I think it's the right place for people to push on it. The guarantee is about what's recoverable from the representation at that moment, not about what a model under optimization pressure will do next.

r001.rationale: It says LEACE rules out linear recovery but nonlinear combinations may still reveal the concept.

r002.rationale: It cites the linear representation hypothesis and says much of what transformers use downstream is linearly accessible.

r003.rationale: It says erasure can change behavior as desired, but does not identify the erased feature as optional or nonessential.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish removing linearly accessible information from preventing a network from using a concept altogether. LEACE gives you a strong guarantee about the first: after erasure, a linear predictor can’t recover the concept from those representations. And it does that while changing the representations as little as possible.

But the rest of a neural network generally isn’t linear. It could exploit information that’s still encoded nonlinearly, or reconstruct the concept in a later layer. So I wouldn’t interpret LEACE as a guarantee that the network can no longer rely on the concept. It’s a useful intervention for investigating that reliance, but you also need to look at what happens to the model’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says information may remain encoded nonlinearly and that the network could exploit it.

r002.rationale: It does not say interpretability research suggests neural networks often use linear representations.

r003.rationale: It does not express hope that erasing an optional, nonessential feature will reduce reliance on it.

sol-6.1.text:
LEACE gives you a fairly precise but limited guarantee: after erasure, the concept can’t be recovered by a linear predictor from those representations. It does that with the smallest possible change to the representations, in a particular mathematical sense.

But that’s not the same as guaranteeing that a neural network can’t rely on the concept. A nonlinear network could recover information that a linear probe can’t, and subsequent layers could reconstruct the concept from other features. So I’d distinguish linear guardedness from actually preventing the model from using something. LEACE guarantees the former; the latter requires stronger assumptions or further evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says LEACE blocks linear recovery but nonlinear networks may still recover and exploit the concept.

r002.rationale: It does not mention interpretability research or that neural networks often use linear representations.

r003.rationale: It expresses no hope about reducing reliance on an optional, nonessential feature by erasing its linearly available information.
